questions.q: What locking granularity does InnoDB use, compared to MyISAM?
options: InnoDB locks at the row level; MyISAM locks the entire table on write
InnoDB locks the entire table; MyISAM locks at the row level
Both lock at the row level
Neither engine uses locking at all
questions.explain: InnoDB's row-level locking lets concurrent writers touch different rows without blocking; MyISAM's table-level locking serializes all writers.

questions.q: What happens to a FOREIGN KEY clause in a MyISAM CREATE TABLE statement?
options: It is accepted syntactically but silently ignored — no referential integrity is enforced
It causes an immediate syntax error
It is enforced exactly like in InnoDB
MyISAM converts it automatically into a CHECK constraint
questions.explain: MyISAM has no foreign key support; the clause is parsed but not enforced.

questions.q: Why might a MyISAM table require REPAIR TABLE after an unclean server shutdown?
options: MyISAM lacks InnoDB's redo-log-based automatic crash recovery
REPAIR TABLE is required after every MySQL restart, regardless of engine
InnoDB also requires REPAIR TABLE in this situation
MyISAM tables cannot be repaired once corrupted
questions.explain: InnoDB replays its redo log automatically on restart; MyISAM has no equivalent mechanism and can need manual repair.

questions.q: Since which MySQL version has InnoDB been the default storage engine?
options: MySQL 5.5
MySQL 8.0
MySQL 4.0
InnoDB has never been the default; it must always be specified explicitly
questions.explain: MySQL made InnoDB the default starting with version 5.5, released in 2010.

questions.q: Per this lesson's honest recommendation, when is MyISAM still a defensible choice?
options: For narrow cases like a static, read-only, single-writer table where table-level locking never actually contends with anything
For any table with high concurrent write traffic
For any table that needs foreign key enforcement
MyISAM should never be used under any circumstances
questions.explain: The lesson frames InnoDB as the near-universal default, with MyISAM defensible only in narrow, low-contention, non-transactional scenarios.
